summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation.

Article 1:221 of that code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold recorded in the sources; they contain no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act, and recorded that the campaign had run two and a half years, with openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

GlobalGayz records that the Aruban government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until that position was challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands. The same report describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes Catholic influence as the main brake on further change.

Harassment has nonetheless occurred. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.
tangentialFactors:
The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning the feeling of being safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking rather than independent evidence, but it documents how the island is positioned to arriving visitors.

Several gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and the Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, the last of which is quoted as saying that Aruba has always been accepting as long as it is not in their face, that people are out but discreetly out, and that there has never been anything official.

The regional comparison recorded in the sources is that Aruba acted ahead of its neighbours: neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed same-sex unions in September 2016, and GlobalGayz describes Aruba's out population as smaller and quieter than Curaçao's.
localsOnly:
Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba.

Openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016, after a two-and-a-half-year campaign that gathered a petition of nearly 20,000 signatures through Igualdad Aruba.

The Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, has been the principal institutional brake on further LGBT legal change, and Catholic influence is identified in the sources as the main obstacle to wider acceptance.

The Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba describes local social norms as acceptance conditioned on discretion: people are out, but discreetly out, with nothing official having been declared.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, name or marker changes on passports and identity documents, or entry and visa screening for transgender travellers. Whether Aruban document practice follows the Netherlands's rules on these points is unresolved here and is not stated by any of the sources.

The 2012 criminal code's discrimination grounds are recorded as covering sexual orientation only, with gender identity and gender expression unaddressed; the inventory contains no finding on whether any separate hate-crime or hate-speech provision reaches gender identity, so that question is unresolved.

The sources record no trans-specific violence, no policing or protection-machinery findings, and no data on access to healthcare or to gender-affirming care for visitors. The harassment documented concerns a same-sex couple's marriage litigation between 2004 and 2007, not incidents involving transgender people.

The claim that Aruba is one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands rests on destination marketing and cultural reporting rather than independent monitoring, and the tourism board's safety positioning is a self-description by the island's own marketer.
